##### **1.3 Historical Generations of Operating Systems** The evolution of operating systems is governed by transitions in underlying physical hardware: every major decrease in component size and increase in circuit density forced corresponding architectural redesigns in system software. ###### **1.3.1 The First Generation (1945–1955): Vacuum Tubes and Plugboards** The earliest electronic digital computers, such as **Colossus** (designed by Alan Turing) and the **ENIAC** (designed by William Mauchly), were built with vacuum tubes and physical plugboards. These room-sized mainframes lacked an operating system entirely: * **Execution model:** A single programmer had exclusive access to the machine for a reserved block of time. Programs were entered manually in mechanical language by physically wiring plugboards or setting switches. * **Hardware constraints:** Systems exhibited high electricity consumption, generated extreme heat requiring massive dedicated air conditioning installations, possessed severely limited memory capacity (a few kilobytes), and suffered frequent tube burnouts. ###### **1.3.2 The Second Generation (1955–1965): Transistors and Batch Systems** The invention of the transistor yielded smaller, more reliable computers that consumed less electricity and generated substantially less heat. Memory architectures transitioned to magnetic core memory, supplemented by secondary storage on magnetic tapes and magnetic disks. To eliminate the enormous human setup delay between consecutive runs, computer manufacturers introduced the **batch system**. Instead of allowing individual programmers interactive physical access: 1. Operators collected programs on punched cards in batches. 2. The cards were transferred to magnetic tape using an auxiliary, inexpensive computer. 3. The main computer loaded a resident monitor—the earliest form of an operating system—which automated job sequencing by reading a job from the input tape, compiling and running it, writing output to a separate tape, and automatically initiating the next job without mechanical intervention. 4. Programming languages shifted from raw binary wiring to symbolic assembly language and early high-level languages. ###### **1.3.3 The Third Generation (1965–1980): Integrated Circuits to Microprocessors** The third generation split across two distinct phases of silicon integration. **Part 1 (1965–1971): Small/Medium Scale Integration (SSI & MSI)** Solid-state integrated circuits allowed multiple transistors onto a single silicon die, reducing power consumption and cost. Representative platforms included the IBM System/360 and 370/168 series, the Honeywell-6000 series, the PDP (Programmed Data Processor) family, and the TDC-316. This era introduced three fundamental software abstractions: * **Multiprogramming:** Partitioning main memory into several regions, each holding a distinct job. When the currently executing job blocks on an I/O operation, the CPU switches to another resident job rather than idling. * **Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line):** Reading jobs directly from punched cards onto magnetic disks as soon as they arrive, and routing output to disk buffers before printing, decoupling slow electromechanical peripherals from CPU scheduling. * **Time-sharing:** A variant of multiprogramming in which the CPU rapidly allocates discrete time slices among multiple concurrent, interactive users at remote terminals, giving each the illusion of having a dedicated computer. The conceptual boundary between multiprogramming and time-sharing is precise: **multiprogramming** manages concurrent job residency to maximize CPU and hardware resource utilization, whereas **time-sharing** multiplexes CPU execution intervals among multiple concurrent human users. Consequently, all time-sharing systems are multiprogramming systems, but not all multiprogramming systems are time-sharing systems. **Part 2 (1971–1980): Large and Very Large Scale Integration (LSI & VLSI)** The emergence of microprocessors integrated thousands of transistors onto a single chip, driving portable computers, high-speed secondary storage memories, RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) data storage architectures, and digital data communications. Operating systems expanded to coordinate parallel processing, simulations, multimedia, virtual reality, speech recognition systems, and artificial intelligence workloads. ###### **1.3.4 The Fourth Generation (1980–1990): Personal Computers** LSI technology allowed complete central processing units to fit on desktop boards. The microcomputer market emerged with machines combining the **Intel 8080** 8-bit microprocessor with an 8-inch floppy disk drive. * **CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers):** Written by Gary Kildall, CP/M was the first dominant disk-based operating system for microcomputers, managing floppy disk files and providing terminal console control. * **The IBM PC:** In 1981, IBM entered personal computing with the IBM PC architecture and contracted Microsoft to supply the operating system (DOS), establishing low-cost single-user personal computing as an industry standard. ###### **1.3.5 The Fifth Generation (1990–Present): Mobile and Ubiquitous Computing** Starting in the 1990s, computing migrated from desktop workstations to battery-powered handheld and mobile devices. Hardware miniaturization progressed from bulky cellular phones to integrated smartphones, personal digital assistants (PDAs), and wearable nodes.
